accepted_variants: A vector of commodity quantities.
cards.definition: A commodity vector lists quantities of defined goods in separate coordinates. A commodity may be distinguished by location, date, quality, or state of the world when those distinctions matter to the model.
major_error_concepts: Combining economically distinct dated goods in one coordinate without an aggregation assumption.
cards.prompt: What is Commodity Vector? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: One coordinate per specified commodity.
Commodity definitions determine what counts as distinct.

accepted_variants: A particular combination of goods for consumption.
cards.definition: A consumption bundle is a feasible candidate vector of goods consumed by an individual. In a standard model it belongs to a consumption set such as the nonnegative orthant.
major_error_concepts: Equating a bundle with the prices of its goods.
cards.prompt: What is Consumption Bundle? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Vector of consumption quantities in the consumption set.

accepted_variants: The agent's initial resource bundle.
cards.definition: An endowment is the vector of resources or goods initially owned by an agent. In a pure exchange model its market value at prices p is p dot omega and finances consumption.
major_error_concepts: Treating endowment quantities as identical to monetary wealth at every price vector.
cards.prompt: What is Endowment? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Initial ownership vector.
Its value depends on market prices.

accepted_variants: The vector of market exchange prices.
cards.definition: A price vector assigns a unit price to each commodity. The cost of bundle x is the dot product p dot x, using consistent commodity and monetary units.
major_error_concepts: Adding prices without multiplying by quantities to value a bundle.
cards.prompt: What is Price Vector? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: One unit price per commodity.
Dot product gives expenditure.

accepted_variants: The consumer's budget resources.
cards.definition: Wealth or income in a static consumer problem is the purchasing-power bound m available for expenditure. It may be taken as exogenous or derived from endowment value and profit income, depending on the model.
major_error_concepts: Assuming monetary income is necessarily independent of prices in an endowment economy.
cards.prompt: What is Wealth and Income? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Monetary expenditure capacity.
Its source is model-dependent.

accepted_variants: A binary ordering of consumption alternatives.
cards.definition: A preference relation x weakly preferred to y states that the consumer regards x as at least as good as y. Strict preference and indifference are derived by comparing the relation in both directions.
major_error_concepts: Equating preference with observed affordability.
cards.prompt: What is Preference Relation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Ranking of bundles as at least as good.
Distinguish weak preference, strict preference, and indifference.

accepted_variants: No pair of alternatives is left unranked.
cards.definition: Preferences are complete if any two feasible bundles can be compared: x is weakly preferred to y, y is weakly preferred to x, or both. Completeness allows indifference.
major_error_concepts: Claiming completeness forbids ties.
cards.prompt: What is Preference Completeness? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Every pair is comparable.
Both directions may hold.

accepted_variants: Internally consistent ranking without preference cycles of the prohibited kind.
cards.definition: Preferences are transitive if x weakly preferred to y and y weakly preferred to z imply x weakly preferred to z. This is a consistency condition across comparisons.
major_error_concepts: Confusing transitivity with a preference for variety.
cards.prompt: What is Preference Transitivity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Chain of weak comparisons implies the corresponding endpoint comparison.

accepted_variants: Small changes do not cause discontinuous ranking jumps.
cards.definition: Continuity of preferences means upper and lower contour sets are closed in the standard finite-dimensional formulation. Informally, a strict preference is robust to sufficiently small changes in bundles.
major_error_concepts: Assuming lexicographic preferences satisfy ordinary Euclidean continuity.
cards.prompt: What is Preference Continuity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Closed weak contour sets, or equivalent open strict-comparison behavior.
Topology of the consumption set matters.

accepted_variants: No bundle is a local satiation point.
cards.definition: Local nonsatiation means every neighborhood of any feasible bundle contains a strictly preferred feasible bundle. It does not require more of each good always to be better.
major_error_concepts: Equating local nonsatiation with positive marginal utility for every good everywhere.
cards.prompt: What is Local Nonsatiation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Arbitrarily nearby improvement exists.
Weaker than strict monotonicity.

accepted_variants: A more-is-better ordering under the stated convention.
cards.definition: Monotone preferences regard coordinatewise larger bundles as at least as good. Strict monotonicity requires an appropriate strict improvement when some quantity increases without any decreasing; the chosen weak or strict convention should be stated.
major_error_concepts: Applying monotonicity to a modeled bad without changing its commodity interpretation.
cards.prompt: What is Monotone Preferences? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: More of goods, with none reduced, does not worsen the bundle.
Distinguish weak and strict monotonicity.

accepted_variants: u(t x+(1-t)y)>min(u(x),u(y)) for x!=y and 0<t<1 on a convex domain.
cards.definition: On a convex consumption set, preferences are strictly convex when, for any distinct bundles x and y with x weakly preferred to y and any 0<t<1, the mixture t x+(1-t)y is strictly preferred to y. Equivalently, a representing utility is strictly quasiconcave. If a maximizer on a convex budget set exists, this condition rules out two distinct maximizers; it does not prove existence.
major_error_concepts: Equating strictly convex preferences with a strictly convex utility function.
Requiring a mixture to be strictly better than both endpoints even when one endpoint is already strictly preferred.
cards.prompt: What is Strictly Convex Preferences? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: For distinct x and y with x weakly preferred to y, every nontrivial mixture is strictly preferred to y.
This is strict quasiconcavity of a representation, not strict convexity of utility, and uniqueness is conditional on existence.

accepted_variants: A weak preference for diversified combinations.
cards.definition: Preferences are convex if each upper contour set is convex: mixtures of bundles at least as good as a reference bundle remain at least as good as it. A representing utility function is then quasiconcave, not necessarily concave.
major_error_concepts: Equating convex preferences with a convex utility function.
cards.prompt: What is Convex Preferences? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Convex upper contour sets.
Mixtures preserve weak desirability.

accepted_variants: A numerical representation of a preference relation.
cards.definition: A utility function represents preferences if u(x) >= u(y) exactly when x is weakly preferred to y. The numbers encode rankings; existence and regularity require appropriate assumptions on preferences and the choice space.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every arbitrary preference relation has a continuous real-valued utility representation.
cards.prompt: What is Utility Representation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Utility inequalities match preference comparisons.
Representation is an ordering device.

accepted_variants: Utility as an order index.
cards.definition: Ordinal utility records only preference order, not meaningful numerical utility differences or ratios. Any strictly increasing transformation preserves the represented ordering.
major_error_concepts: Inferring twice as much satisfaction from a utility number twice as large.
cards.prompt: What is Ordinal Utility? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Rankings, not cardinal distances, are meaningful.

accepted_variants: An order-preserving reindexing of utility.
cards.definition: A strictly increasing transformation v = phi composed with u preserves all utility rankings. It may alter derivatives and curvature while representing the same preferences.
major_error_concepts: Using an arbitrary nonmonotonic transformation and claiming preferences are unchanged.
cards.prompt: What is Increasing Utility Transformation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Strictly increasing scalar transformation preserves comparisons.
Numerical curvature need not be preserved.

accepted_variants: An equivalence set of equally ranked bundles.
cards.definition: An indifference set contains bundles the consumer regards as equally good as a reference bundle. For a utility representation it is a level set u(x) = constant; in two goods it is often drawn as an indifference curve.
major_error_concepts: Treating bundles above and below the utility level as indifferent.
cards.prompt: What is Indifference Set? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Bundles equivalent in preference.
Utility level set when a representation exists.

accepted_variants: A weak-preference superlevel set.
cards.definition: The upper contour set of x consists of all bundles weakly preferred to x. With utility u it is the superlevel set {y: u(y) >= u(x)}.
major_error_concepts: Using u(y) <= u(x) as the upper contour set.
cards.prompt: What is Upper Contour Set? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Bundles at least as good as the reference.

accepted_variants: The local willingness-to-trade ratio; curve slope is -MU1/MU2.
cards.definition: For differentiable two-good utility with nonzero marginal utility of good 2, the marginal rate of substitution of good 1 for good 2 is MU1/MU2. It is the amount of good 2 the consumer is locally willing to give up for one additional unit of good 1 along an indifference curve.
major_error_concepts: Equating MRS to the ratio of total quantities consumed.
cards.prompt: What is Marginal Rate of Substitution? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Marginal-utility ratio under differentiability.
Distinguish the positive tradeoff convention from the negative indifference-curve slope.

accepted_variants: The feasible consumption set under the spending limit.
cards.definition: The budget set is the set of consumption bundles affordable at prices p and wealth m: {x in X: p dot x <= m}. Its shape also depends on the consumption set and price assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Including only bundles that exhaust the budget in the budget set.
cards.prompt: What is Budget Set? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Affordable bundles satisfy the expenditure inequality.

accepted_variants: The spending-boundary line.
cards.definition: The budget line in a two-good model is the set p1 x1 + p2 x2 = m. With positive prices its slope is -p1/p2 and its intercepts are m/p1 and m/p2.
major_error_concepts: Confusing the whole affordable region with its boundary line.
cards.prompt: What is Budget Line? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Budget-exhausting equality.
Relative-price slope with positive prices.

accepted_variants: The primal consumer choice problem.
cards.definition: The utility maximization problem chooses the most preferred affordable bundle: maximize u(x) over the budget set. Existence and uniqueness are separate questions governed by the feasible set and preferences.
major_error_concepts: Maximizing utility without imposing the resource constraint.
cards.prompt: What is Utility Maximization? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Maximize utility subject to affordability.
Do not assume uniqueness automatically.

accepted_variants: Ordinary or uncompensated demand.
cards.definition: Marshallian demand is the bundle or set of bundles solving utility maximization at prices p and income m. It is also called uncompensated demand because nominal income is held fixed in ordinary price comparisons.
major_error_concepts: Confusing it with minimum-expenditure demand at a fixed utility target.
cards.prompt: What is Marshallian Demand? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Utility-maximizing choice as a function or correspondence of prices and income.

accepted_variants: Achievable utility as a function of market parameters.
cards.definition: The indirect utility function v(p,m) is the maximum utility attainable at prices p and wealth m. It is the optimized value rather than the chosen bundle.
major_error_concepts: Identifying indirect utility with the demand vector.
cards.prompt: What is Indirect Utility? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Value of the utility maximization problem.

accepted_variants: The dual consumer problem.
cards.definition: The expenditure minimization problem chooses the cheapest bundle achieving a target utility: minimize p dot x subject to u(x) >= u_bar. The target is utility, not a fixed nominal spending allowance.
major_error_concepts: Maximizing utility subject to a target expenditure and calling it expenditure minimization.
cards.prompt: What is Expenditure Minimization? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Minimize spending while reaching target utility.

accepted_variants: Compensated demand.
cards.definition: Hicksian demand is the cost-minimizing bundle or correspondence at given prices and target utility. It describes compensated choice holding utility fixed.
major_error_concepts: Holding nominal income fixed when defining Hicksian demand.
cards.prompt: What is Hicksian Demand? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Minimizer of spending for a fixed utility level.

accepted_variants: The value function of expenditure minimization.
cards.definition: The expenditure function e(p,u_bar) is the minimum spending needed to reach utility u_bar at prices p. It is homogeneous of degree one in prices and concave in prices under the standard fixed feasible-target formulation.
major_error_concepts: Calling e a utility measure or an income-independent chosen bundle.
cards.prompt: What is Expenditure Function? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Optimized minimum expenditure.
Depends on prices and utility target.

accepted_variants: A derivative identity connecting indirect utility and ordinary demand.
cards.definition: Roy's identity recovers Marshallian demand from differentiable indirect utility: x_i(p,m) = -(partial v/partial p_i)/(partial v/partial m), where the denominator is nonzero and standard regularity conditions hold.
major_error_concepts: Omitting the minus sign or using expenditure-function derivatives instead.
cards.prompt: What is Roy's Identity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Negative price derivative divided by income derivative.
Differentiability and nonzero income derivative.

accepted_variants: Envelope recovery of compensated demand.
cards.definition: Shephard's lemma identifies the price derivative of a differentiable expenditure function with Hicksian demand: partial e/partial p_i = h_i. The analogous result for a differentiable cost function gives conditional input demand.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting this derivative as uncompensated demand at an arbitrary fixed income.
cards.prompt: What is Shephard's Lemma? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Price derivative of optimized expenditure equals compensated quantity.
Use differentiability or the appropriate correspondence version.

accepted_variants: Substitution-income decomposition of Marshallian price response.
cards.definition: The Slutsky equation decomposes an ordinary price effect into a compensated substitution effect and an income effect: partial x_i/partial p_j = partial h_i/partial p_j - x_j partial x_i/partial m, evaluated at the matching utility level.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the ordinary own-price effect must always have the compensated effect's sign.
cards.prompt: What is Slutsky Equation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Compensated derivative minus the purchasing-power income term.
Evaluate the primal and dual choices at matching utility.

accepted_variants: A good with positive income elasticity on the stated range.
cards.definition: A normal good has demand that rises with income, holding prices fixed, over the range being considered. The classification can change across income levels.
major_error_concepts: Defining normality by the own-price response rather than income response.
cards.prompt: What is Normal Good? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Positive income-demand response at fixed prices.

accepted_variants: A good with negative income elasticity locally.
cards.definition: An inferior good has demand that falls as income rises, holding prices fixed, over the relevant range. Inferiority concerns income response, not low quality or necessarily unusual price behavior.
major_error_concepts: Equating all inferior goods with Giffen goods.
cards.prompt: What is Inferior Good? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Negative income-demand response at fixed prices.

accepted_variants: A good obeying the ordinary own-price demand pattern.
cards.definition: An ordinary good has downward-sloping uncompensated own-price demand over the range considered: its demand falls when its own price rises with income and other prices fixed.
major_error_concepts: Confusing ordinary with normal; income and own-price classifications differ.
cards.prompt: What is Ordinary Good? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Negative Marshallian own-price response.

accepted_variants: An upward-sloping Marshallian own-price demand good.
cards.definition: A Giffen good has demand increasing with its own price at fixed nominal income and other prices. Under standard consumer assumptions this requires an inferior-good income effect large enough to outweigh the compensated substitution effect.
major_error_concepts: Calling every inferior or prestige-priced good Giffen without the income-substitution mechanism.
cards.prompt: What is Giffen Good? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Positive uncompensated own-price response.
Strong opposing income effect under standard preferences.

accepted_variants: Substitution in ordinary demand.
cards.definition: Goods i and j are gross substitutes in the indicated direction when Marshallian demand for i rises as the price of j rises, holding income and other prices fixed. Gross cross-price effects need not be symmetric.
major_error_concepts: Assuming gross-substitute cross effects must be symmetric because compensated derivatives are symmetric.
cards.prompt: What is Gross Substitutes? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Positive uncompensated cross-price derivative.
Direction and fixed-income convention matter.

accepted_variants: Complementarity in ordinary demand.
cards.definition: Goods i and j are gross complements in the indicated direction when Marshallian demand for i falls as the price of j rises, with income and other prices fixed. The classification includes income effects.
major_error_concepts: Equating gross complementarity automatically with a particular indifference-curve shape.
cards.prompt: What is Gross Complements? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Negative uncompensated cross-price response.

accepted_variants: The wealth component of a price response.
cards.definition: The income effect is the demand change attributable to a change in purchasing power. In a price-change decomposition, compensation separates this effect from substitution while keeping the chosen compensation convention explicit.
major_error_concepts: Assuming an income effect always raises demand for every good.
cards.prompt: What is Income Effect? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Demand response from purchasing-power change.
Sign depends on normal or inferior behavior.

accepted_variants: The utility-compensated price response.
cards.definition: The substitution effect is the demand response to changed relative prices with utility compensated in the Hicksian version. Under standard convex preferences, compensated own-price demand is nonincreasing.
major_error_concepts: Holding nominal income unchanged and calling the full response purely substitution.
cards.prompt: What is Substitution Effect? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Relative-price response with utility held fixed by compensation.
Own compensated effect is nonpositive under standard assumptions.

accepted_variants: A set-valued representation of production possibilities.
cards.definition: A production set is the set of feasible net-output vectors. Outputs are commonly positive coordinates and inputs negative coordinates, allowing technological feasibility to be described without assuming a single output.
major_error_concepts: Treating every negative net-output coordinate as a financial loss rather than an input.
cards.prompt: What is Production Set? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Feasible net-input/output combinations.
State the sign convention.

accepted_variants: The firm's feasible transformation possibilities.
cards.definition: A technology describes which input-output transformations are feasible. It can be represented by a production set, an input requirement set, or a production function when the relevant assumptions allow it.
major_error_concepts: Equating technology with output prices or profitability.
cards.prompt: What is Technology? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Feasibility of input-output transformations.
Different mathematical representations serve different settings.

accepted_variants: An attainable production plan.
cards.definition: A feasible input-output vector belongs to the production set and can be implemented with the given technology. Feasibility alone does not imply technical efficiency or profit maximization.
major_error_concepts: Calling every feasible production plan optimal.
cards.prompt: What is Feasible Production Plan? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Membership in the technological feasible set.
Separate feasibility from efficiency and optimality.

accepted_variants: The single-output production frontier.
cards.definition: A production function q = f(z) gives maximal output attainable from an input vector z in a specified single-output technology. It describes a technological boundary rather than a market supply rule.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting all observed production below the frontier as technological impossibility.
cards.prompt: What is Production Function? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Maximum output from specified inputs.
Technological relation, not price-based supply.

accepted_variants: A production-function level set.
cards.definition: An isoquant is the set of input combinations yielding the same output level under a production function. It shows technological substitution among inputs, not equality of input costs.
major_error_concepts: Confusing an isoquant with an isocost line.
cards.prompt: What is Isoquant? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Equal-output input combinations.

accepted_variants: The local extra output per unit of an input.
cards.definition: The marginal product of an input is the additional output from a marginal increase in that input while other inputs are fixed. For a differentiable production function it is the corresponding partial derivative.
major_error_concepts: Equating marginal product with average output per total input.
cards.prompt: What is Marginal Product? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Output derivative with respect to one input, holding others fixed.

accepted_variants: The local input substitution rate at constant production.
cards.definition: The marginal technical rate of substitution of input 1 for input 2 is MP1/MP2 where the denominator is nonzero. It gives the local amount of input 2 that can be saved per additional input 1 while output stays constant; the isoquant slope is its negative.
major_error_concepts: Using market input prices to define the technological rate itself.
cards.prompt: What is Technical Rate of Substitution? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Marginal-product ratio along an isoquant.
Tradeoff keeps output fixed.

accepted_variants: More-than-proportional output response to proportional input expansion.
cards.definition: Increasing returns to scale mean proportionally scaling every input by t greater than one increases maximal output by more than t: f(tz) > t f(z) over the stated range. This differs from changing only one input.
major_error_concepts: Inferring increasing returns solely from increasing marginal product of one input.
cards.prompt: What is Increasing Returns to Scale? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: All inputs scaled together.
Output rises more than proportionally.

accepted_variants: Proportional output scaling.
cards.definition: Constant returns to scale mean f(tz) = t f(z) for positive scale factors in the relevant domain. Scaling all inputs scales maximal output by the same factor.
major_error_concepts: Confusing constant returns to scale with constant marginal product for each input separately.
cards.prompt: What is Constant Returns to Scale? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Degree-one homogeneity in all inputs.

accepted_variants: Diminishing output response to scale expansion.
cards.definition: Decreasing returns to scale mean f(tz) < t f(z) when all inputs are scaled by t greater than one over the considered range. The output response is less than proportional.
major_error_concepts: Treating decreasing returns to scale as synonymous with diminishing marginal returns to one variable input.
cards.prompt: What is Decreasing Returns to Scale? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: All-input proportional increase gives less-than-proportional output.

accepted_variants: A constrained-adjustment production horizon.
cards.definition: The short run is a planning horizon in which at least one relevant input or capacity choice is fixed. Its length is defined by adjustment opportunities, not a universal calendar duration.
major_error_concepts: Defining the short run as exactly one year in all industries.
cards.prompt: What is Short Run? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Some input or capacity is fixed.
Technological or contractual horizon rather than a fixed number of months.

accepted_variants: The full-adjustment planning horizon.
cards.definition: The long run is a planning horizon in which all relevant modeled inputs or capacities can be adjusted. It differs from the short run by the set of adjustable choices, not by a universal time cutoff.
major_error_concepts: Assuming long run means uncertainty disappears or all costs are zero.
cards.prompt: What is Long Run? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: All modeled input choices adjustable.

accepted_variants: The conditional producer input-choice problem.
cards.definition: Cost minimization chooses the least expensive input bundle capable of producing a target output at given input prices. It holds the output target fixed rather than choosing the profit-maximizing output simultaneously.
major_error_concepts: Treating the target output as unconstrained in the same minimization.
cards.prompt: What is Cost Minimization? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Minimize input expenditure subject to production of the target.

accepted_variants: Minimum production expenditure as a function of prices and output.
cards.definition: The cost function c(w,q) is the minimum input expenditure needed to produce output q at input prices w. It reflects both technology and input prices and can differ between short-run and long-run constraints.
major_error_concepts: Confusing total accounting expenditure on an inefficient plan with the minimum cost function.
cards.prompt: What is Cost Function? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Value of the least-cost production problem.

accepted_variants: Output-invariant cost for the specified decision horizon.
cards.definition: Fixed cost is cost independent of the chosen output quantity over the relevant range and horizon. A fixed cost may be avoidable by shutting down or entering differently; fixed and sunk are not synonymous.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every fixed cost is irrecoverable and irrelevant to every decision.
cards.prompt: What is Fixed Cost? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Does not vary with current output over the stated range.
Distinguish fixed from sunk.

accepted_variants: The cost attributable to variable production choices.
cards.definition: Variable cost changes with the output quantity or associated variable inputs. In the usual decomposition total cost equals fixed plus variable cost for the specified horizon.
major_error_concepts: Treating variable cost as necessarily linear in output.
cards.prompt: What is Variable Cost? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Output-dependent component of cost.

accepted_variants: Unit cost.
cards.definition: Average cost is total cost divided by output for positive output: AC(q) = C(q)/q. Average variable cost and average fixed cost divide the corresponding components by output.
major_error_concepts: Equating average cost with the derivative of cost.
cards.prompt: What is Average Cost? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Cost per unit of positive output.

accepted_variants: Incremental cost of marginal production.
cards.definition: Marginal cost is the local increase in minimum cost caused by an additional unit of output, MC = partial C/partial q when differentiable. It is distinct from average cost.
major_error_concepts: Using C(q)/q as marginal cost by definition.
cards.prompt: What is Marginal Cost? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Output derivative of the cost function.

accepted_variants: Optimal net earnings from a feasible production choice.
cards.definition: Profit maximization chooses a feasible production plan maximizing revenue minus cost at the prices and market conditions faced by the firm. Interior first-order conditions require additional assumptions to identify a global maximum.
major_error_concepts: Maximizing output regardless of costs and calling it profit maximization.
cards.prompt: What is Profit Maximization? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Maximize revenue minus costs subject to feasibility.
First-order equality alone does not establish global optimality.

accepted_variants: Optimal producer output response.
cards.definition: A supply correspondence assigns the profit-maximizing output choices to given prices and other parameters. It becomes a function when the optimum is unique; shutdown and nonconvexities can create corners or multiple optima.
major_error_concepts: Assuming supply must equal every point on marginal cost, including loss-making or dominated choices.
cards.prompt: What is Supply Correspondence? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Set of profit-maximizing supplied quantities.
Function requires uniqueness.

accepted_variants: Cost-minimizing input demand.
cards.definition: Conditional factor demand is the input bundle minimizing cost for specified input prices and output. It differs from unconditional profit-maximizing input demand because output is held fixed.
major_error_concepts: Allowing output to adjust freely while calling the resulting demand conditional on output.
cards.prompt: What is Conditional Factor Demand? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Least-cost inputs conditional on target output.

accepted_variants: Envelope identity for the profit value function.
cards.definition: Hotelling's lemma recovers optimal net output from derivatives of a differentiable profit function with respect to commodity prices. Under the net-output sign convention, an input-price derivative is the negative of input demand.
major_error_concepts: Claiming profit must increase with an input price because all derivatives are positive demands.
cards.prompt: What is Hotelling's Lemma? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Profit derivative equals optimal net-output quantity.
Input signs follow the net-output convention.

accepted_variants: A producer without modeled price-setting power.
cards.definition: A competitive firm takes relevant market prices as given when choosing production. In a differentiable interior output choice with suitable optimality conditions, price equals marginal cost; the firm still must compare feasible alternatives and shutdown.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a competitive firm chooses the market price to maximize its profit.
cards.prompt: What is Competitive Firm? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Price taking.
Interior price-equals-marginal-cost condition is conditional, not the complete solution.

accepted_variants: The operating-versus-shutdown profitability condition.
cards.definition: A firm shuts down when producing yields lower profit than its feasible shutdown option. In the standard short-run model with unavoidable fixed cost and avoidable variable cost, positive production requires revenue to cover variable cost; the familiar threshold is minimum average variable cost under standard assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Using average total cost as the short-run shutdown threshold when fixed costs are unavoidable.
cards.prompt: What is Shutdown Condition? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Compare production profit with shutdown profit.
Specify which costs are avoidable.

accepted_variants: The competitive no-excess-profit condition in the appropriate constant-returns or entry setting.
cards.definition: With constant returns to scale and competitive prices, positive profit could be expanded without bound when scale is unrestricted. A finite active equilibrium therefore has zero profit under the standard feasibility assumptions; free entry supplies a related no-positive-profit condition when entry is available.
major_error_concepts: Claiming all firms in all markets earn zero accounting profit.
cards.prompt: What is Zero-Profit Condition? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Unrestricted constant-returns scaling rules out finite positive-profit optimum.
Free entry and cost assumptions matter.

accepted_variants: A price equating modeled demand and supply with other markets fixed.
cards.definition: A partial-equilibrium price clears one modeled market while prices and conditions in other markets are held fixed or treated as exogenous. It does not simultaneously solve every market in the economy.
major_error_concepts: Treating partial equilibrium as automatically a full general equilibrium.
cards.prompt: What is Partial-Equilibrium Price? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Market-clearing price within a single-market or restricted-market model.
Other conditions held outside the equilibrium calculation.

accepted_variants: The unsatisfied net demand quantity.
cards.definition: Excess demand is demand minus available supply at a given price. A positive value indicates desired purchases exceed supply at that price; it is not itself a completed allocation of goods.
major_error_concepts: Calling actual sales greater than available supply excess demand.
cards.prompt: What is Excess Demand? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Demand minus supply.
Positive sign denotes a shortage at the stated price.

accepted_variants: The unsold desired supply imbalance.
cards.definition: Excess supply is supply minus demand at a given price. A positive value indicates that suppliers wish to sell more than buyers wish to purchase at that price.
major_error_concepts: Using demand minus supply while retaining the excess-supply sign convention.
cards.prompt: What is Excess Supply? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Supply minus demand.
Positive sign denotes a surplus at the stated price.

accepted_variants: An economy of consumption and trade without firms transforming resources.
cards.definition: A pure exchange economy consists of consumers, preferences, and initial commodity endowments without modeled production. Trade reallocates the aggregate endowment among consumers.
major_error_concepts: Adding newly produced resources while calling the same model pure exchange.
cards.prompt: What is Exchange Economy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Consumers exchange fixed total endowments.
No production in the pure exchange model.

accepted_variants: The economy-wide distribution of resources and production choices.
cards.definition: An allocation specifies a consumption bundle for every consumer and, when production is modeled, relevant production plans. It describes who receives what, not merely the prices used to trade.
major_error_concepts: Equating an allocation with a single consumer's budget line.
cards.prompt: What is Allocation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Assignment of bundles across agents.

accepted_variants: An allocation within the economy's resource possibilities.
cards.definition: A feasible allocation respects aggregate resource constraints. In pure exchange with free disposal, the sum of consumption bundles cannot exceed the aggregate endowment coordinatewise; without disposal the appropriate equality is imposed.
major_error_concepts: Calling an individually affordable allocation feasible without checking aggregate resources.
cards.prompt: What is Feasible Allocation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Aggregate consumption respects available resources.
Disposal convention determines inequality versus equality.

accepted_variants: A feasible allocation that cannot be unanimously improved with at least one strict gain.
cards.definition: An allocation is Pareto efficient if no feasible reallocation makes at least one person strictly better off without making anyone worse off. Efficiency does not establish fairness or a unique distribution.
major_error_concepts: Claiming Pareto efficiency means equal consumption or maximum utility for every individual separately.
cards.prompt: What is Pareto Efficiency? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: No feasible Pareto improvement.
Separate efficiency from distributional judgments.

accepted_variants: A graphical representation of a two-by-two exchange economy.
cards.definition: An Edgeworth box depicts feasible allocations of two goods between two consumers with fixed aggregate quantities. Each consumer measures consumption from an opposite origin, allowing preferences and mutually beneficial trades to be visualized in the same diagram.
major_error_concepts: Allowing the box dimensions to vary while holding the aggregate endowment fixed.
cards.prompt: What is Edgeworth Box? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Two consumers and two goods with fixed total resources.
Opposite origins encode complementary allocations.

accepted_variants: The efficient locus of the exchange box.
cards.definition: The contract curve is the set of Pareto-efficient allocations in an Edgeworth box. Smooth interior efficient allocations typically equalize the consumers' MRS values; boundary efficient allocations require separate consideration.
major_error_concepts: Defining the entire contract curve only by interior tangencies and ignoring possible boundary allocations.
cards.prompt: What is Contract Curve? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Set of Pareto-efficient allocations.
Interior tangency is a conditional characterization.

accepted_variants: A Walrasian price-allocation equilibrium.
cards.definition: A competitive equilibrium is a price vector and feasible allocation at which consumers optimize subject to their budgets, firms optimize if present, and markets clear. Choices are individually optimal at common prices and jointly compatible.
major_error_concepts: Calling a price vector an equilibrium without checking optimal choices or market clearing.
cards.prompt: What is Competitive Equilibrium? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Individual optimization at common prices.
Feasibility and market clearing.

accepted_variants: The economy's net-demand map.
cards.definition: An aggregate excess-demand function gives total desired consumption minus total available supply as a function of prices and other specified parameters. In exchange economies individual wealth typically changes with the value of endowments when prices change.
major_error_concepts: Holding all endowment incomes fixed by default while claiming an unrestricted exchange-economy price response.
cards.prompt: What is Aggregate Excess-Demand Function? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Aggregate desired purchases net of resources or supply.
Endowment-valued income may vary with prices.

accepted_variants: No unmatched desired trades under the equilibrium conditions.
cards.definition: Market clearing means chosen aggregate demand matches available supply in each traded market. With free disposal, zero-priced goods may permit excess supply under the model's complementarity conditions.
major_error_concepts: Claiming any price necessarily clears the market because realized purchases equal realized sales.
cards.prompt: What is Market Clearing? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Compatibility of aggregate demand and supply.
Free-disposal and zero-price conventions can matter.

accepted_variants: The efficiency theorem for competitive equilibrium.
cards.definition: The First Welfare Theorem states that a competitive equilibrium is Pareto efficient under assumptions including local nonsatiation and the relevant complete-market, price-taking, and no-externality environment. It does not say the resulting allocation is equitable.
major_error_concepts: Applying the conclusion automatically in the presence of unpriced externalities or market power.
cards.prompt: What is First Welfare Theorem? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Competitive equilibrium implies Pareto efficiency under its assumptions.
Efficiency is not fairness.

accepted_variants: Supporting efficient allocations with prices and transfers.
cards.definition: The Second Welfare Theorem gives conditions under which a Pareto-efficient allocation can be supported by competitive prices after suitable lump-sum redistribution. Convexity and supporting-price assumptions are central; equilibrium versus quasi-equilibrium refinements require care.
major_error_concepts: Claiming arbitrary distortionary taxes automatically implement every efficient allocation.
cards.prompt: What is Second Welfare Theorem? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Efficiency can be decentralized after suitable redistribution under convexity and regularity assumptions.
Redistribution must not distort the modeled marginal incentives.

accepted_variants: A centralized resource-allocation optimization benchmark.
cards.definition: A social planner problem selects a feasible allocation to meet a specified welfare objective or utility constraints. It is an analytical benchmark whose solution depends on the objective and information assumptions, not a unique distribution selected by feasibility alone.
major_error_concepts: Assuming all planners or welfare weights yield the same allocation.
cards.prompt: What is Social Planner Problem? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Optimize a stated social objective over feasible allocations.
Objective or welfare weights must be specified.

accepted_variants: An exogenous shift used in comparative statics.
cards.definition: A parameter change alters an exogenous input to a model, such as a tax rate, income, technology coefficient, or endowment. Comparative statics compares the resulting equilibria or optima while stating what else is held fixed.
major_error_concepts: Treating an endogenous equilibrium price as independently changed without specifying the intervention or new equilibrium problem.
cards.prompt: What is Parameter Change? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Change an exogenous model input.
State the fixed variables and comparison.

accepted_variants: Comparative-statics movement of the equilibrium.
cards.definition: An equilibrium response is the change in equilibrium variables induced by a parameter change. Local derivatives require a regular equilibrium branch; multiplicity or bifurcation can make a single smooth response undefined.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a unique smooth response in a model with unselected multiple equilibria.
cards.prompt: What is Equilibrium Response? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Endogenous changes after an exogenous shift.
Local derivative requires a suitable equilibrium selection and regularity.

accepted_variants: Mechanism-based comparative-statics accounting.
cards.definition: A sign-and-mechanism decomposition separates a response into economically interpretable channels and determines their signs under explicit assumptions. An ambiguous total sign can result when channels oppose each other.
major_error_concepts: Assigning a universal sign after showing only one of several relevant channels.
cards.prompt: What is Comparative-Statics Decomposition? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Identify channels and assumptions behind their signs.
Opposing effects can leave the total ambiguous.

accepted_variants: A policy-imposed gap between transaction prices received and paid.
cards.definition: A per-unit tax introduces a wedge between the buyer's payment and the seller's receipt. In a standard competitive partial-equilibrium model, the incidence depends on demand and supply responses rather than solely on which side remits the payment.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the legally named payer necessarily bears the entire economic burden.
cards.prompt: What is Per-Unit Tax? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Buyer-seller price wedge.
Economic incidence differs from statutory remittance.

accepted_variants: A payment tied to units purchased or produced.
cards.definition: A per-unit subsidy creates a wedge that raises the seller's effective receipt relative to the buyer's net payment when applied to a transaction. Its equilibrium effects depend on the supply-demand environment and how it is funded and implemented.
major_error_concepts: Treating the subsidy payment as a free resource with no financing or opportunity-cost consideration.
cards.prompt: What is Per-Unit Subsidy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Payment support creates a buyer-seller effective-price wedge.
Effects depend on the model's responses and funding assumptions.

accepted_variants: An upper price constraint.
cards.definition: A price ceiling is a legal maximum price. In the standard competitive supply-demand model a ceiling below the unconstrained equilibrium is binding and can create excess demand, requiring some nonprice allocation mechanism.
major_error_concepts: Claiming a ceiling above the unconstrained equilibrium must change that equilibrium.
cards.prompt: What is Price Ceiling? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Maximum permitted price.
Binding below the relevant unconstrained equilibrium.

accepted_variants: A lower price constraint.
cards.definition: A price floor is a legal minimum price. In the standard competitive supply-demand model a floor above the unconstrained equilibrium is binding and can create excess supply unless another mechanism absorbs or limits it.
major_error_concepts: Confusing a price floor with a maximum allowable price.
cards.prompt: What is Price Floor? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Minimum permitted price.
Binding above the relevant unconstrained equilibrium.

accepted_variants: A constraint-induced gap between notional demand and actual access.
cards.definition: A rationing wedge is a gap between desired and obtainable choices caused by quantity limits or nonprice allocation rules. When prices do not clear a market, posted prices alone no longer describe every consumer's effective opportunity set.
major_error_concepts: Assuming each buyer can purchase their full desired quantity at a binding controlled price.
cards.prompt: What is Rationing Wedge? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Allocation restrictions alter attainable choices.
Posted prices may not fully summarize access.

accepted_variants: Utility levels are preference indices rather than measured satisfaction units.
cards.definition: Ordinal utility comparisons are meaningful within the represented preference order, but utility differences and ratios have no invariant interpretation under all increasing transformations. Interpersonal welfare comparisons require additional assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Subtracting two people's arbitrary ordinal utility numbers and treating the result as a measured welfare gap.
cards.prompt: What is Limits of Ordinal Utility? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Only ranking is invariant.
Interpersonal cardinal comparison is not supplied by ordinal representation alone.

accepted_variants: Order-preserving utility transformations preserve choices.
cards.definition: Replacing utility u by any strictly increasing phi(u) leaves the set of maximizing bundles unchanged on the same feasible set. The transformation must preserve strict ordering; differentiability is not required for this choice-invariance statement.
major_error_concepts: Requiring an affine transformation for ordinary ordinal consumer-choice invariance.
cards.prompt: What is Utility Transformation and Choice? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Same feasible set and strictly increasing transformation.
Argmax set is unchanged.

accepted_variants: A positive-bundle optimum away from consumption-set corners.
cards.definition: An interior consumer optimum has strictly positive choices in all nonnegativity-constrained goods, so no such constraint is active. Under differentiability, local nonsatiation, and regularity, budget-constrained first-order conditions equate marginal utility per unit of price across goods.
major_error_concepts: Declaring an interior stationary point globally optimal without preference or curvature conditions.
cards.prompt: What is Interior Consumer Optimum? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: No binding zero-consumption constraints.
Marginal conditions require the stated regularity.

accepted_variants: Indifference curve and budget line are tangent at a regular interior solution.
cards.definition: At a differentiable regular interior optimum with a binding budget and positive prices, MRS = p1/p2. This is a tangency condition; corners and nonsmooth preferences need different optimality descriptions.
major_error_concepts: Forcing tangency at a corner or kink.
cards.prompt: What is Consumer Tangency Condition? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: MRS equals relative price under interior differentiable conditions.
Not a universal condition for every optimum.

accepted_variants: A boundary optimum.
cards.definition: A corner solution lies on a boundary such as zero consumption of a good. It can be optimal when a feasible move into the interior does not improve the objective; equal-MRS tangency need not hold.
major_error_concepts: Rejecting a corner simply because MRS does not equal the price ratio there.
cards.prompt: What is Corner Solution? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Optimum at a feasible-set boundary.
Interior first-order equalities need not apply.

accepted_variants: KKT optimality conditions for constrained consumer or firm choice.
cards.definition: Kuhn-Tucker conditions include stationarity, primal and dual feasibility, and complementary slackness for inequality-constrained optimization. They replace unrestricted interior tangencies at active constraints, subject to constraint qualification and appropriate sufficiency assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every point satisfying KKT is a global optimum in an arbitrary nonconvex problem.
cards.prompt: What is Kuhn–Tucker Conditions? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Stationarity, feasibility, and complementary slackness.
Necessary and sufficient roles depend on regularity and convexity assumptions.

accepted_variants: No money illusion in the standard budget-based consumer model.
cards.definition: Marshallian demand is homogeneous of degree zero in all prices and income: scaling p and m by the same positive factor leaves the budget set and choices unchanged. This is a nominal-unit invariance.
major_error_concepts: Scaling prices alone and claiming demand must stay unchanged.
cards.prompt: What is Demand Homogeneity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Scale every price and income together.
Affordable bundles remain identical.

accepted_variants: Individual budget balance or individual Walras-law identity.
cards.definition: Under budget exhaustion, individual demand satisfies p dot x(p,m) = m. In an exchange setting with wealth p dot omega, the individual's valued net demand is p dot (x-omega) = 0; local nonsatiation commonly supplies budget exhaustion under standard positive-price assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the identity implies each commodity's excess demand is individually zero.
cards.prompt: What is Individual Walras' Law? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Spending equals wealth under budget exhaustion.
Endowment-valued net demand then has zero value.

accepted_variants: Maximum-theorem regularity of consumer choice.
cards.definition: Under the hypotheses of a maximum theorem, such as continuity of utility and a suitably continuous compact feasible correspondence, optimal-value functions are continuous and optimizer correspondences are upper hemicontinuous. A unique optimizer then often gives continuous demand on the regular domain.
major_error_concepts: Claiming continuous utility alone guarantees globally continuous single-valued demand.
cards.prompt: What is Demand Continuity Conditions? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Continuity result needs compactness and feasible-set regularity.
Set-valued and unique-choice conclusions differ.

accepted_variants: A unique consumer optimum under strict convexity assumptions.
cards.definition: A strictly quasiconcave utility representation on a convex budget set gives at most one maximizing bundle when an optimum exists. Strictly convex preferences provide the corresponding ordinal condition; existence remains separate.
major_error_concepts: Assuming weak convexity alone always rules out multiple optimal bundles.
cards.prompt: What is Demand Uniqueness Conditions? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Strict preference convexity and convex feasibility support uniqueness.
Uniqueness does not prove existence.

accepted_variants: Consumer expenditure-utility duality.
cards.definition: Under standard monotonicity and duality conditions, e(p,v(p,m)) = m and v(p,e(p,u)) = u on the relevant attainable range. At matching values, Hicksian and Marshallian choices coincide where the selections are well defined.
major_error_concepts: Equating Hicksian and Marshallian demand without matching income and utility.
cards.prompt: What is Consumer Duality Identities? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Primal and dual value functions invert the wealth-utility relationship at fixed prices.
Matching conditions and attainable targets matter.

accepted_variants: The Slutsky matrix's symmetry and nonpositive quadratic forms.
cards.definition: Under smooth regular consumer duality, the substitution matrix is the price Hessian of the expenditure function. It is symmetric and negative semidefinite because the expenditure function is concave in prices; these properties concern compensated, not arbitrary gross, price effects.
major_error_concepts: Applying symmetry directly to all Marshallian cross-price derivatives without the income corrections.
cards.prompt: What is Substitution Matrix Properties? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Compensated derivative matrix is symmetric and negative semidefinite.
Regularity and expenditure concavity supply the result.

accepted_variants: Preference information inferred from observable choice behavior.
cards.definition: Observed choices from known feasible sets impose restrictions on preferences that could rationalize them. Revealed-preference tests use affordability and chosen bundles, but finite observations generally do not identify a unique full utility representation.
major_error_concepts: Treating one purchase as proof of an unrestricted preference ordering over every unobserved bundle.
cards.prompt: What is Revealed-Preference Restrictions? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Choices restrict rationalizing preferences.
Partial identification rather than automatic uniqueness.

accepted_variants: Decentralized allocation through common price signals.
cards.definition: Prices coordinate decentralized choices by entering consumer budgets and firms' revenue-cost comparisons. A competitive equilibrium requires the independently chosen plans to be mutually feasible and market-clearing, not merely individually optimal.
major_error_concepts: Assuming individual optimization automatically makes aggregate markets clear at arbitrary prices.
cards.prompt: What is Price Coordination? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Common prices guide separate budget and profit decisions.
Market compatibility is an additional equilibrium condition.

accepted_variants: Conditional sign predictions from economic primitives.
cards.definition: A comparative-statics sign follows from assumptions on primitives such as preferences, technology, constraints, and equilibrium regularity. When these assumptions change, even the direction of the response can change.
major_error_concepts: Presenting a special-case derivative sign as an assumption-free law.
cards.prompt: What is Conditional Comparative-Statics Signs? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: State the assumptions producing the sign.
No universal direction without supporting restrictions.

accepted_variants: Value-function sensitivity at an optimum.
cards.definition: The envelope theorem differentiates an optimized value by the direct parameter effect on the objective, with constraint effects included through the appropriate Lagrangian. It avoids differentiating the optimizer explicitly when the requisite regularity conditions hold.
major_error_concepts: Ignoring a changing constraint when applying an unconstrained envelope formula.
cards.prompt: What is Envelope Theorem? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Differentiate the objective or Lagrangian at the optimum with respect to the parameter.
Parameter-dependent constraints must be included.

accepted_variants: Local comparative statics by implicit differentiation.
cards.definition: For equilibrium equations F(z,theta)=0 with an invertible Jacobian F_z, the implicit function theorem gives a local response dz/dtheta = -F_z^-1 F_theta. Singularity can prevent this smooth local characterization.
major_error_concepts: Using the inverse formula when the equilibrium Jacobian is singular.
cards.prompt: What is Implicit Equilibrium Response? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Invertible endogenous-variable Jacobian.
Negative inverse-Jacobian sensitivity formula.

accepted_variants: Existence of a utility index representing a regular preference ordering.
cards.definition: Preference representation theorems give conditions under which an ordering admits a real-valued, often continuous, utility function. Completeness, transitivity, continuity, and properties of the consumption space are central; monotonicity can add useful structure but does not replace all other assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Claiming monotonicity alone guarantees a continuous utility representation for every relation.
cards.prompt: What is Utility Representation Theorems? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Representation requires stated preference and domain hypotheses.
Continuous utility is a stronger conclusion than arbitrary numerical representation.

accepted_variants: A condition ensuring multiplier-based first-order characterization is applicable.
cards.definition: A constraint qualification is a regularity condition that allows a local constrained optimum to be represented by valid Lagrange or KKT multipliers. It is distinct from convexity assumptions that can make those conditions sufficient for global optimality.
major_error_concepts: Treating the existence of a Lagrangian as proof that constraint qualification holds.
cards.prompt: What is Constraint Qualification? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Regularity supports necessary multiplier conditions.
Separate constraint qualification from global sufficiency.

accepted_variants: Curvature defined by values at convex combinations.
cards.definition: A concave function lies above chords between graph points; a convex function lies below them. Utility concavity is stronger than the quasiconcavity associated with convex preferences, and increasing transformations need not preserve concavity.
major_error_concepts: Interchanging convex utility and convex preferences.
cards.prompt: What is Concavity and Convexity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Correct chord inequalities.
Distinguish function concavity from convex preferences.

accepted_variants: The derivative matrix of the gradient.
cards.definition: The Hessian is the matrix of second partial derivatives of a scalar function. Under twice continuous differentiability it is symmetric; its quadratic form describes local second-order curvature.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a positive Hessian proves a utility maximum rather than a local minimum in an unconstrained problem.
cards.prompt: What is Hessian? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Second-derivative matrix.
Quadratic form captures directional curvature.

accepted_variants: A matrix construction for constrained second-order conditions.
cards.definition: A bordered Hessian combines objective or Lagrangian second derivatives with gradients of equality constraints. It is one way to assess second-order curvature on feasible tangent directions; determinant sign rules depend on the convention and number of constraints.
major_error_concepts: Applying one memorized determinant sign rule to every constraint count and sign convention.
cards.prompt: What is Bordered Hessian? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Includes constraint gradients and second-order information.
Tests constrained rather than arbitrary directions.

accepted_variants: Conditions that turn stationarity into a valid optimum claim.
cards.definition: A sufficient optimality condition guarantees that a candidate is optimal. For example, maximizing a concave objective over a convex feasible set allows appropriate first-order or KKT conditions to establish a global maximum; strict concavity can establish uniqueness.
major_error_concepts: Treating zero first derivatives alone as sufficient in a nonconvex problem.
cards.prompt: What is Sufficient Optimality Conditions? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Sufficient conditions imply optimality, not merely candidacy.
Concavity and convex feasibility support global conclusions.

accepted_variants: WARP, excluding direct revealed-preference reversals.
cards.definition: The weak axiom of revealed preference rules out a two-choice reversal: if x is chosen while a distinct y is affordable, y cannot later be chosen with x affordable in a way contradicting the revealed comparison, under the specified choice convention.
major_error_concepts: Inferring a violation when the previously chosen bundle is not affordable in the later budget.
cards.prompt: What is Weak Axiom of Revealed Preference? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Affordability-based two-observation consistency.
Observed feasibility, not utility numbers, drives the test.

accepted_variants: SARP, the no-cycle condition for revealed-preference chains.
cards.definition: The strong axiom of revealed preference rules out reversals of indirectly revealed preference obtained by chaining observed choices. It strengthens the weak axiom by addressing cycles involving more than two observations.
major_error_concepts: Checking only two-observation reversals and claiming a complete strong-axiom test.
cards.prompt: What is Strong Axiom of Revealed Preference? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Transitive revealed-preference chains cannot be reversed inconsistently.
Stronger than direct pairwise restrictions.

accepted_variants: Reconstructing consumer choice from valid primal or dual representations.
cards.definition: Consumer duality can recover demand or preferences from suitably regular expenditure or indirect-utility functions and recover those value functions from the primal problem. Such recovery requires integrability and shape restrictions, not an arbitrary fitted derivative field.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every collection of demand equations integrates to well-behaved preferences.
cards.prompt: What is Primal–Dual Recovery? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Primal and dual descriptions recover each other under regularity.
Shape and integrability conditions restrict admissible dual functions.

accepted_variants: Preferences with straight income expansion paths through the origin.
cards.definition: Homothetic preferences have indifference sets that are radial expansions of one another and can be represented by an increasing transformation of a degree-one homogeneous function under standard conditions. At fixed prices, unique demands scale proportionally with income on the standard cone domain.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every convex preference ordering is homothetic.
cards.prompt: What is Homothetic Preferences? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Scale-consistent preferences.
Proportional income scaling of demand under the stated conditions.

accepted_variants: The parallel Engel-curve structure underlying Gorman aggregation.
cards.definition: Gorman polar indirect utility has the form v_i(p,m_i)=a_i(p)+b(p)m_i with a common income slope across consumers. Under the standard regularity conditions this supports aggregation of demand using total income rather than its distribution, with the appropriate normalization.
major_error_concepts: Assuming arbitrary heterogeneous income slopes permit aggregation independent of income distribution.
cards.prompt: What is Gorman Polar Form? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Affine indirect utility in income with a common slope function.
Common slope is essential for distribution-independent aggregation.

accepted_variants: Limits of treating heterogeneous consumers as one optimizing household.
cards.definition: A representative consumer is an aggregate modeling device, not generally a literal average person whose preferences reproduce every individual tradeoff. Exact aggregation and welfare interpretations require additional restrictions on heterogeneity and income distribution.
major_error_concepts: Assuming any aggregate demand can be interpreted as a normatively meaningful average consumer.
cards.prompt: What is Representative-Consumer Limits? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Aggregate device requires explicit aggregation assumptions.
Aggregate demand representation does not automatically justify welfare comparisons.

accepted_variants: Weak aggregate restrictions despite well-behaved individual preferences.
cards.definition: The Sonnenschein-Mantel-Debreu results show that aggregate excess demand can have very flexible shapes even when individuals satisfy standard rationality assumptions. Basic aggregate restrictions such as continuity, homogeneity, and Walras' law do not generally ensure a unique or stable equilibrium.
major_error_concepts: Claiming rational consumers alone guarantee a unique downward-sloping aggregate excess-demand system.
cards.prompt: What is Aggregate Excess-Demand Flexibility? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Individual rationality leaves aggregate excess-demand shape broadly unrestricted.
Uniqueness and stability need extra structure.

accepted_variants: Existence through a Brouwer- or Kakutani-type argument under suitable hypotheses.
cards.definition: Equilibrium existence arguments often formulate a self-consistent price-choice problem as a fixed point. Continuity or upper hemicontinuity, convexity, compactness, and nonempty choice sets enable the relevant fixed-point theorem; they do not by themselves give uniqueness.
major_error_concepts: Equating an existence theorem with a constructive unique equilibrium algorithm.
cards.prompt: What is Fixed-Point Equilibrium Intuition? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Equilibrium as a self-consistent fixed point.
The theorem's domain and correspondence assumptions matter.

accepted_variants: The competitive limit of the core under appropriate large-economy conditions.
cards.definition: Core-equivalence results relate allocations immune to blocking coalitions to competitive equilibrium as economies become large under suitable replication, convexity, and regularity assumptions. They do not identify the core with competitive allocations in every small finite economy.
major_error_concepts: Claiming every two-person exchange economy has a core consisting of one competitive allocation.
cards.prompt: What is Core-Equivalence Intuition? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Large-economy connection between coalitional stability and competition.
Finite-economy equality is not automatic.

accepted_variants: The geometric role of convexity in choice and equilibrium.
cards.definition: Convexity matters because mixtures remain feasible or acceptable, supporting separation, supporting prices, and stable optimization structure. Nonconvex preferences or technologies can undermine standard existence or decentralization arguments without making every equilibrium impossible.
major_error_concepts: Claiming one nonconvexity logically rules out all possible equilibria.
cards.prompt: What is Role of Convexity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Mixture closure supports optimization and supporting-price arguments.
Loss of convexity weakens theorems rather than proving universal failure.

accepted_variants: Market coverage of all modeled contingencies and commodities.
cards.definition: Complete markets provide trade opportunities for every commodity or contingent claim relevant to the model's allocation problem. Missing markets can prevent mutually beneficial reallocations and invalidate standard complete-market efficiency conclusions.
major_error_concepts: Equating complete markets with every person having unlimited income.
cards.prompt: What is Role of Complete Markets? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Relevant goods or state-contingent claims are tradable.
Missing markets restrict feasible private trades.

accepted_variants: Parametric treatment of market prices by each agent.
cards.definition: Price taking means agents treat prices as fixed when selecting their own quantities. It underlies competitive first-order conditions and welfare arguments; a price-setting agent faces a different revenue or opportunity relation.
major_error_concepts: Using price-equals-marginal-cost as an unrestricted monopoly optimum condition.
cards.prompt: What is Role of Price Taking? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Agents do not internalize an effect of their own quantity on market price in the model.
Market-power problems differ from competitive choice.

accepted_variants: The scope limits of a one-period known-environment model.
cards.definition: A static certainty model abstracts from time-dependent adjustment and unresolved future states. Applying its conclusions requires checking whether saving, investment, risk, information, or transition costs are important to the actual question.
major_error_concepts: Treating a static equilibrium comparison as a full prediction of the path or risk of adjustment.
cards.prompt: What is Limits of Static Certainty Models? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
required_concepts: Static certainty omits dynamic and uncertain dimensions.
